title: Smoke seen from a mile away as army detonates US stockpile of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
summary: Controlled blast to dispose of lead azide risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in 100-mile radius

blocks.text: The US Army detonated the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, moving ahead after multiple delays and despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.
A reporter nearby for local news station KWQC reported seeing a large amount of smoke from more than a mile away.

The controlled blast was to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the bomb-making chemicals stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people. The explosion risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed as the weather forecast changes.

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said that it has been on the ground in Iowa before the detonation, and that they will continue to be there during and “as long as necessary after” to “ensure communities are safe”.

“EPA will continue our monitoring efforts during the scheduled, controlled detonation, along with immediate and continuous post-event sampling and subsequent remediation as necessary following the detonation,” the agency said.
On Tuesday, the army released new maps forecasting that the projected path will move south-west of Middletown before extending into northern Missouri.

The army has warned: “All people, but especially infants, children, pregnant women, adults and children with chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease, or dementia, should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas until further guidance is provided.”

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), said on Wednesday morning that at Donald Trump’s direction, HHS has “deployed personnel to Iowa to help protect families and support local officials throughout this operation”.
“We will stay on the ground to support the community through the response and recovery,” Kennedy Jr said.
At a press conference on Tuesday, officials said they were not able to find a “viable alternative” after the material was discovered to be dangerously unstable earlier this year.

“There is consensus across experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance,” said Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US army.
In a statement on Tuesday, Josh Turek said he had been briefed on the detonation, adding that the chemicals “should never have been allowed to degrade to this point”.

“I will continue asking questions about how we got here. There is no excuse for such a failure of transparency and communication, especially when the health and safety of the public is involved,” the senator-elect said.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) is supporting “relocation for all residents of Middletown, Iowa, and immediate surrounding impacted areas”, according to the army, “out of an abundance of caution”.

In a social media post, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said: “Fema will ensure every resident who needs to temporarily evacuate will receive the support they need, including transportation, lodging, meals and other essential assistance.”
“We’ve made it very clear to those who are within a south-westerly location: if they choose to relocate, we will offer services,” said Cameron Hamilton, the Fema administrator, in a statement.

The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) activated an emergency response to support the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services to “provide accurate public health communication and technical assistance to our state and federal partners”.

In a statement, the CDC said that at the request of the state of Iowa, it will support the state’s health department to develop “recommendations to help protect people from potential exposure to lead and air pollution” and in preparing to support the state with any “any post-event community health assessment needs”.
The CDC also said that it was “activating a multidisciplinary team with expertise in toxicology, communications, and public health emergency response.”

The organization on Tuesday urged residents to “pay attention to alerts related to the detonation”, and to stay indoors or evacuate “if you are in the evacuation zone, until state officials indicate that the air is safe to return home”.
They told residents to “close all doors and windows in your home” and to “seal any gaps to prevent outdoor air from coming indoors”.

On Tuesday, Kim Reynolds, issued a proclamation of disaster emergency for Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren counties. With Reynolds’s approval, the Iowa national guard is providing up to 100 federally activated soldiers to support public safety and community outreach efforts around the detonation.

“Iowa agencies are actively engaged alongside our federal and local partners, and we remain focused on ensuring communities have the information and resources they need before, during, and after the operation,” Iowa’s governor said in a statement.

An emergency notification sent to phones on Tuesday said that some people within five miles south-west of the plant may be evacuated and warned those up to 20 miles away to remain indoors with windows closed to “avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration”. The army encouraged residents who live outside the recommended evacuation zone to shelter in place.
The operation was initially planned for last Friday, but was rescheduled three times as public concern grew and environmentalists sued to block the detonation.
Trump ordered the military to hold off on detonation pending a court ruling and a signoff from the Democratic governor-elect, Rob Sand, who does not take office until January.

On Monday, a three-judge panel of the eighth circuit court of appeals said the army could proceed with detonating the stockpile, finding that the Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards in an emergency permit to minimize the dispersal of dust.
